ru/graphStatsPanel.json::graphStatsPanel: Mean number of edges per node (in + out). Higher values indicate a more interconnected graph.
Average number of hops between all reachable pairs of nodes. Lower values indicate a tighter, more navigable graph ('small world' property).
Number of disconnected subgraphs. More than one means some nodes cannot reach others by any path. Ideally this is 1 for a unified data model.
Ratio of actual edges to the maximum possible edges. Near 0 = sparse; near 1 = fully connected. Most real-world graphs are sparse (<0.01).
Longest shortest path between any two reachable nodes. Measures how 'wide' the graph is. A high diameter means some entities are many hops apart.
Total number of relationships between nodes.
Breakdown of relationship count by relationship type.
Nodes with no edges at all. In a data model these are orphaned entities with no modeled relationships — usually a data quality gap.
Percentage of nodes in the biggest connected subgraph. Low values mean your data is fragmented — entities that should be related aren't linked yet.
Degree of the most connected node — the top hub. A very high max relative to average suggests a hub-and-spoke structure.
Total number of nodes (entities) in the current graph.
Breakdown of node count by entity type.
Nodes with the most connections. These are the most central entities in the graph — joins or traversals through them reach the widest set of neighbors.

Invite the person into the root organization from its Team page.
They sign in and redeem the invitation, which makes them a member of root.
Assign them the platform_admin role in root — that is what confers deployment-wide administration.

Signing in made you this deployment's platform_admin — you hold every capability here, and nobody else can claim the role now. You are also the administrator of the root organization, which already carries the demo sources, tables, and domains.

From the next sign-in onward, anyone who authenticates creates their own organization. They are never made a platform administrator by signing in, and inviting people into their org is their own work as its org_admin.

ru/tableEditForm.json::tableEditForm.all: How long to wait past the boundary for inputs to be fresh-through the window before closing the period.
ru/tableEditForm.json::tableEditForm.bit: Append-only bitemporal history. off = ordinary materialization (each refresh replaces the data; no history). snapshot = each refresh appends the whole fresh dataset stamped with its system time; simplest and works on any engine, but storage grows by full size per refresh. delta = each refresh appends only the rows the engine computes as changed, plus tombstones for removed keys; smaller, and needs an entity key. Either way no row is ever updated to retire it — 'as of' history is derived at read time from the immutable append log. Efficiency varies by engine.

Comma-separated column(s) identifying the ENTITY being tracked (e.g. customer_id) — the identity each new version belongs to. If this MV keeps multiple states of the same entity — over time, or along any other dimension — that entity appears on many rows, so the entity key is NOT unique in the table and therefore is NOT the primary key — the row's PK is a surrogate (or entity + system-time). Used to reconstruct state 'as of' a time: partition by this key and take the latest version at that time. Required for delta mode (no key means no delta); in snapshot mode it groups versions for as-of reconstruction.
ru/tableEditForm.json::tableEditForm.cac: How long query results for this table are cached in memory. 0 disables caching. Leave blank to inherit the source-level TTL. Reduces load on the source database for frequently-queried tables.
ru/tableEditForm.json::tableEditForm.cal: The month/day the fiscal year begins (e.g. Oct 1 for US federal). Quarters group three calendar months from here; the year is labeled by the calendar year it ends in.
Dates with no business-day window (with the weekend set). Versioned and immutable per calendar version, so a replay reproduces the same window existence. Only affects a business-day grain.
The reference start date of a 4-4-5 retail year. Must fall on the chosen week-start weekday; weeks are the atom (13-week quarters, 4/4/5-week periods).
Weekdays treated as non-business days for business-day-grain gating (default Saturday + Sunday).
The registered snapshot-boundary calendar. Declaring one makes this MV periodic; leave empty for the live/NRT default.
Select a calendar (or leave empty for live)

needs the source's CDC transport (bootstrap servers, topic prefix) — configure it on the

ru/tableEditForm.json::tableEditForm.cha: How Provisa learns rows changed. ttl = refresh on the Cache TTL timer; probe = source-native freshness query, re-pull only on change; ttl_probe = probe after the TTL floor elapses; native/debezium/kafka = source push. Inherit = follow the source-level default.
ru/tableEditForm.json::tableEditForm.con: per-instance — each instance its own copy

Only matters when Provisa runs as several instances behind a load balancer. It decides whether the materialized view is ONE copy shared by all instances, or a separate copy per instance. Shared: a single copy in the shared store, refreshed by one instance at a time (a short lease with fencing), so every instance reads the same consistent snapshot — pick this when instances must agree. Per-instance: each instance builds and refreshes its own copy independently — simpler and faster, but instances can briefly disagree (eventually consistent), so only safe for a deterministic view over a source that's stable within a refresh cycle. Where the copy lives depends on the federation engine's store: per-instance only makes sense when each instance has its OWN store (e.g. an embedded/in-process DuckDB). With a SHARED external store (Postgres, Trino + object store, a warehouse) every instance writes the same physical table, so use shared — per-instance has nowhere private to write and would just clobber.
shared — one copy, all instances agree
ru/tableEditForm.json::tableEditForm.dat: (publish to catalog / export to Atlas, Atlan, etc.)
ru/tableEditForm.json::tableEditForm.des: Human-readable description shown in the API schema (SDL), data catalog, and AI-assisted query generation. Good descriptions improve auto-generated SQL accuracy.
ru/tableEditForm.json::tableEditForm.exp: The preflight gate: the period is closed only once its inputs are fresh-through the window boundary. Default = every SQL-lineage input. Uncheck to name a custom set (or none = calendar-only, verify nothing).
ru/tableEditForm.json::tableEditForm.fre: Source-native query returning one comparable token; blank → MAX(watermark). Provisa compares stored vs. fresh by equality and re-pulls only on change.
ru/tableEditForm.json::tableEditForm.gra: When a version is cut: a nesting period (daily…annual), or a custom Outlook/iCalendar recurrence.
ru/tableEditForm.json::tableEditForm.inc: Apply the input's reported changes to the prior landed state instead of re-running the query — the classic way to keep a derived table cheaply in sync with a source's change stream (CDC), applying its inserts/updates by key each refresh rather than recopying the whole source. It maintains CURRENT state (no versions). The same change stream commonly feeds a SEPARATE history table too: this incremental table is the live mirror, while a Time Travel delta MV off the same deltas appends each change as a new version — one stream, two tables (current + full history). Requires a primary key and an incrementalizable view; an infeasible declaration is rejected at registration.
ru/tableEditForm.json::tableEditForm.loa: Shield a load-sensitive source: serve this table entirely from a scheduled snapshot so queries never hit the source. Requires at least one refresh gate — an off-peak window, a cache TTL cadence, or a probing change signal. Inherit = follow the source-level default.
ru/tableEditForm.json::tableEditForm.loc: This deployment uses an embedded federation engine and materializes into an instance-local store. If you are running more than one instance, each instance keeps its own copy of this view and they may briefly differ until they converge (eventual consistency). To have every instance read one shared copy, set a shared materialization store (a central Store URL in Settings) or use a different federation engine. A single instance is unaffected.
ru/tableEditForm.json::tableEditForm.mat: Precompute THIS view's SQL into a stored cache table (CTAS into mv_cache) on the Refresh Interval below. Distinct from 'Prefer Materialized' above, which pulls a raw source table into the store — this materializes a Provisa-defined view.
ru/tableEditForm.json::tableEditForm.mvP: Row-identity key (from the Primary Key checkboxes in the columns below):
Comma-separated column(s) identifying a row — required for upsert persistence and for incremental maintenance.
Upsert and incremental maintenance need a row-identity key. Mark the key column(s) as Primary Key in the columns list below.
ru/tableEditForm.json::tableEditForm.nam: Controls how the alias is cased in the API schema. snake_case → my_table, camelCase → myTable, PascalCase → MyTable. 'Inherit' uses the source's convention. Affects GraphQL field names, Cypher labels, and SDL output.
ru/tableEditForm.json::tableEditForm.noP: No primary key set — the receiver can't apply updates or deletes (tombstones) without one. Mark a
ru/tableEditForm.json::tableEditForm.nrt: NRT debounce: a burst of upstream changes collapses into one recompute. Quiet = seconds of calm before firing (0 = real-time). Max delay = the hard staleness cap under continuous churn.
ru/tableEditForm.json::tableEditForm.off: IANA timezone the off-peak window is evaluated in (e.g. UTC, America/New_York). Tracks DST.
Maintenance window as HH:MM-HH:MM (24h). The scheduler refreshes a load-protected table only while this window is open. Leave blank for no window (cadence/probe drive the refresh instead).
ru/tableEditForm.json::tableEditForm.per: How each update is written to the MV's store. Its options depend on Time Travel (keep history): OFF stores current state only — replace (overwrite everything) or upsert (merge by primary key); ON keeps history — snapshot (append the whole fresh result as a new version each refresh) or delta (append only the rows that changed, plus tombstones for deletes). Snapshot/delta are the bitemporal storage modes, which the engine uses in place of replace/upsert.
ru/tableEditForm.json::tableEditForm.pre: Force this table to be materialized into the store and federated from there, instead of reached live. Use when the connector is a poor fit for this table's queries. Inherit = follow the source-level default.

Optional preflight check run after the view SQL and before landing: define preflight(streams, ctx) and return a VERDICT — ctx.ok() to continue, ctx.abort(reason) to reject (error + poison downstream), or ctx.quarantine(reason) to hold without landing. streams is a dict keyed by input node: streams["schema.table"] yields that input's rows lazily, so you inspect an input without materializing it. A check inspects; it does NOT transform rows (put transforms in SQL or an external processor). A SQL-expressible check — if any(...)/all(...) over one input's rows — is pushed down to the engine as a count probe over that input, so it scales to a billion rows; anything else streams each input as Arrow batches and short-circuits. Call ctx.warn(reason) for a non-fatal advisory. It MUST be deterministic — no clock, randomness, imports, or IO — and is purity-checked when you save; a non-deterministic or unsafe check is rejected.
ru/tableEditForm.json::tableEditForm.pro: How the freshness probe detects change, gated by source type. watermark → append (fetch rows past MAX(watermark)); hash → replace (content token, e.g. ETag/checksum); count → replace (row-count delta, coarse); none → replace on cadence (the output content-hash still suppresses an unchanged ripple). Auto = resolve per source class.
ru/tableEditForm.json::tableEditForm.ref: How often the materialized view is rebuilt (CTAS into mv_cache). Governs freshness of the stored table that QUERIES read. Distinct from Cache TTL (which caches query results) and from Poll interval (which paces the live change stream to subscribers).
ru/tableEditForm.json::tableEditForm.sql: The GraphQL/Cypher field name exposed in the API. Defaults to the table name. Changing this renames the entity across all queries and SDL docs.
ru/tableEditForm.json::tableEditForm.ttl: above (neither the table nor the source defines one).
ttl needs a materialized view — enable
above and set a Refresh Interval.
Refreshes every {{sec}}s (from the materialized view's Refresh Interval).
ru/tableEditForm.json::tableEditForm.upd: Keeps history (time travel), compactly. Every refresh appends ONLY the rows that changed (plus tombstones for deletes) as new versions — you can still query 'as of' any time, but storage grows only by the change, not the whole result. The classic way to maintain a full change history / audit trail of a source without storing a full copy each refresh. Needs an entity key to identify the entity across versions.

The query is NOT re-run. The single input delivers the rows that changed (as a delta), and only those rows are merged into the stored table by primary key — so work per refresh scales with the SIZE OF THE CHANGE, not the whole dataset. The cheapest option for large, slowly-changing data. It applies only when all three hold: (1) exactly ONE input (no joins), (2) that input emits a delta — i.e. it runs on a change/CDC signal, not full snapshots, and (3) the view SQL is a plain column projection (no join, filter, GROUP BY, aggregate, DISTINCT, or computed column) so the input's delta maps 1:1 to this view's delta. Also needs a primary key. If a refresh brings no delta (a full-snapshot input or a probe trigger), it falls back to a full recompute for that refresh.

Current state, no history. Every refresh re-runs the whole query and replaces the stored table with the fresh result. Simplest and always correct. Work per refresh scales with the TOTAL size of the inputs, not with how much actually changed.

Keeps history (time travel). Every refresh appends the ENTIRE fresh result as a new version stamped with its time — you can query the table 'as of' any past refresh. Simplest history model and works on any engine, but storage grows by the full result size every refresh.

Current state, no history. Every refresh re-runs the whole query, then merges the result into the stored table by primary key: matching rows are updated in place, new rows inserted, nothing deleted-and-reinserted. The query still recomputes everything, so work scales with total input size — only the write is by key.

ru/tour.json::tour.steps.step0.descripti:
🧭 This compass reopens the tour anytime. Leave whenever — click the app or press Esc.

Provisa is a governed query compiler for federated data that stays out of the data path.

🎯 The whole core is one short exercise: connect some databases, then query them seven ways — or skip the syntax and just ask in plain English. About five minutes, right from your desktop: no servers, no infrastructure to stand up (that comes later, when you're ready).

Natural LanguageSQLGraphQLCyphergRPCJSON:APIRESTMCPPostgres · pgwireNeo4j · BoltJDBC · Java/JVMArrow Flight SQL · ADBCDuckDB · airport

Everything after that — more sources, federation, files, relationships, views, scheduled pipelines — is how you grow with the platform, not what you need on day one. We'll flag where the core ends.

Ready? Let's connect a source. →

ru/tour.json::tour.steps.step2.descripti: ➕ New connections start with this button — PostgreSQL, Snowflake, MongoDB, a REST API, a CSV, and 30+ more.
ru/tour.json::tour.steps.step2.title: Register a source
ru/tour.json::tour.steps.step20.descript:
🔧 Compose your whole delivery pipeline right here — no separate ETL tool:
  • 👁️ Views — over any table, ephemeral or materialized, and views over views.
  • ⚡ Commands — governed, typed operations (an HTTP service, a Python model, a stored procedure) that do double duty: a step inside your pipeline, and a first-class API that downstream apps and agents call to act on your data — invokable from every surface, fully governed and traced.
  • ⭐ Entities & facts — declare a dimension or fact once and Provisa generates the warehouse, methodology-neutral: 3NF (Inmon), star schema (Kimball), or Data Vault.
  • 📏 Metrics — governed aggregate definitions (“net revenue”) with grain bound at query time. Define once; every surface — SQL, GraphQL, AI agents — computes the same number, and views built on a metric regenerate when its definition changes.
ru/tour.json::tour.steps.step20.title: Build your delivery pipeline
ru/tour.json::tour.steps.step21.descript:
🏗️ Materialize a view and you get a full ETL engine, declared not scripted:
  • 📅 Scheduled snapshots on real business calendars — recurrence rules, holidays, business-day gating, and a close grace period, so it fires on your reporting calendar, not just a clock.
  • 🗄️ Store As… — replace, upsert, or keep history with snapshot / delta, plus incremental compute.
  • 🕰️ Time travel — bitemporal history; query the model as of any point in time.
  • ⚡ Near-real-time refresh with debounce, or freshness-driven republish as inputs change.
ru/tour.json::tour.steps.step21.title: Materialize into a live warehouse
ru/tour.json::tour.steps.step22.descript:
🧬 Lineage isn't opaque. This is a real query, analyzed. Each result column is traced back through its transforms — follow name_upper — and joins to the exact source columns that feed it.

Commands are declaratively defined, so every step is captured; materialized views retain full lineage by definition. Nothing runs — the query is only analyzed.

→ Last stop: operating it in production.
ru/tour.json::tour.steps.step22.title: Lineage, end to end
ru/tour.json::tour.steps.step23.descript:
The Admin pages run the platform:
  • ⚙️ Choose and configure your federation engine — pluggable: DuckDB (embedded, zero-config), Trino, PostgreSQL, ClickHouse, or a cloud warehouse as a first-class engine (Snowflake, BigQuery, Databricks, Microsoft Fabric, Azure Synapse). Swap it anytime — the model, the surfaces, and the governance above it never change.
  • 🔗 Whichever engine you pick brings its own live external data reach — Parquet, Iceberg, Delta read in place, zero-copy, credentials auto-provisioned. Anything it can't link live lands as a governed replica.
  • 🔑 Manage encryption keys and wire up auth providers
  • 📊 Full observability — redirect to any OpenTelemetry collector for enterprise-class trace management

The same model travels from local dev to production, validated at every step — no rewrite:

  • Develop — embedded DuckDB, no Docker. Build & validate locally.
  • Validate at scale — Docker, spin up an engine + observability. Prove behavior against production engines.
  • Promote — point at your own infrastructure, build through CI/CD, ship to production.
ru/tour.json::tour.steps.step23.title: Operate it
ru/tour.json::tour.steps.step24.descript:
🎉 You're back where you started. Now make it yours:
  • 1️⃣ Register one of your real sources
  • 2️⃣ Expose a few tables, draw a relationship or two
  • 3️⃣ Query it from Explore in any language:
SQLGraphQLCyphergRPCJSON:APIREST

Point pgwire or Bolt tools at it — everything just works.

📚 The Docs tab has the full guides. 🧭 The compass up top replays this tour anytime. Enjoy Provisa.
ru/tour.json::tour.steps.step24.title: That's the tour — now make it yours
ru/tour.json::tour.steps.step3.descripti:
One connector list spans every category:
  • Databases — PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB, Oracle, SQL Server, Greenplum
  • Cloud warehouses — Snowflake, BigQuery, Databricks, Redshift, Microsoft Fabric, Azure Synapse
  • Analytics / OLAP — ClickHouse, Druid, Pinot
  • Lakes & files — Iceberg, Delta Lake, Hive, Parquet, CSV, JSON
  • NoSQL & graph — MongoDB, Cassandra, Redis, Neo4j
  • APIs — REST, GraphQL, gRPC
  • Streaming — Kafka
  • Enterprise SaaS — SharePoint, Splunk · plus government data subscriptions
Pick one, fill the connection, Save. The list isn't fixed — the native federation engines are extensible: declare a custom Postgres FDW or DuckDB extension in config and Provisa reaches a new source type, no code.
ru/tour.json::tour.steps.step3.title: 35+ source types
ru/tour.json::tour.steps.step4.descripti:
Whatever the source — a Mongo collection, a Kafka topic, a REST endpoint, a graph — Provisa decomposes it into a 2D table: one uniform shape to query across every source.

📁 Group tables into domains, each owned by a data steward who guards the model's quality as it evolves.
ru/tour.json::tour.steps.step4.title: Everything becomes a table
ru/tour.json::tour.steps.step5.descripti:
Choose a source, schema, and table, then pick columns — each with its own policy:
  • 🎭 Masking — redact values per role
  • 👁️ Visibility — show or hide the column
  • 🏷️ Aliases — rename for the model

That's the whole setup — a source and a few tables. 🚀 Now let's query it. →
ru/tour.json::tour.steps.step5.title: Pick columns & policy
ru/tour.json::tour.steps.step6.descripti:
SQL lives in the SQL explorer. Standard SQL federated across every source — join Postgres to Mongo to a CSV in one statement. And the model's own metadata and every activity trace are themselves queryable tables here — join your audit log or lineage straight to live data.

🔌 Not just this explorer — the same governed SQL runs through multiple wire protocols; your tool picks the one it already speaks:

  • pgwire — every Postgres-compatible client — psql, DBeaver, Tableau, Power BI — connects out of the box.
  • JDBC — drops into any Java/JVM app, ETL pipeline, or JDBC-capable BI tool.
  • Arrow Flight SQL — columnar streaming for ADBC clients — no row re-encoding, built for large result sets.
  • DuckDB · airport — ATTACH Provisa from DuckDB and query the governed federation in place.
ru/tour.json::tour.steps.step6.title: SQL (1 of 7 surfaces)
ru/tour.json::tour.steps.step7.descripti:
◈ The same query, typed as GraphQL:

{ inquiries { groupBy { user }, count } }

Grouping and aggregates over your relationships — 🎯 one endpoint, 📖 self-documenting schema.

🔌 Hit it from any GraphQL client — Apollo, Relay, urql — and, with federation enabled, drop Provisa into an Apollo supergraph as a subgraph, so your federated model composes alongside your existing graphs.
ru/tour.json::tour.steps.step7.title: GraphQL (2 of 7 surfaces)
ru/tour.json::tour.steps.step8.descripti:
🕸️ Traverse the federated model as a graph with Cypher:

MATCH (u:Users)-[:SUBMITTED]->(i:Inquiries)

↔️ That traversal runs across sources — no single graph database required.

🔌 And any Bolt client — Neo4j Browser, Bloom — runs that same traversal over the wire, no code change.
ru/tour.json::tour.steps.step8.title: Cypher (3 of 7 surfaces)
ru/tour.json::tour.steps.step9.descripti:
⚙️ Every registered entity is also a gRPC service:

rpc QueryInquiries(...) returns (...)

Call it from any gRPC client — 📐 strongly typed, 🚀 high-throughput.
ru/tour.json::tour.steps.step9.title: gRPC (4 of 7 surfaces)
ru/tour.json::tour.steps.stepPreview.des: 👀 Expand a row and click Preview — live data through the governed pipeline: masked, access-controlled, and server-paged, so even a billion-row table opens instantly. Filters, sorts, and grouping run inside the query, and API-backed tables prompt for their required parameters first.
ru/tour.json::tour.steps.stepReports.des: 📊 The audit log you queried earlier also feeds ready-made reports — usage ranking, PII access, policy denials, query health — each a governed view in the ops domain. Adding your own takes one SQL statement, and it becomes a cataloged, exportable data product like any other table.

ru/adminPage.json::adminPage.enabledHint: Results larger than the threshold are written to object storage and returned as a presigned URL instead of inline rows.
ru/adminPage.json::adminPage.defaultThre: Row count above which a result is redirected to object storage rather than returned in the response.
ru/adminPage.json::adminPage.defaultForm: File format redirected results are written in.
ru/adminPage.json::adminPage.presignedUr: How long the presigned URL for a redirected result stays valid.
ru/adminPage.json::adminPage.domainPrefi: Prepends the domain to generated names, so two domains can expose a table of the same name.
ru/adminPage.json::adminPage.namingConve: Casing applied to GraphQL field names, which Cypher property keys follow as well. Cypher labels are always PascalCase. gRPC, JSON:API and OpenAPI are unaffected — they name each column the way the database spells it.
ru/adminPage.json::adminPage.sqlNamingCo: Casing applied to names on the SQL plane — what the pgwire, Bolt and semantic-SQL surfaces query. Set separately from the GraphQL convention so renaming one plane never renames the other.
ru/adminPage.json::adminPage.domainModeH: Legacy leaves domains inert; Single stores everything under one hidden domain; Namespaced requires a domain on every table. Changing this backs up and resets the configuration.
ru/adminPage.json::adminPage.defaultDoma: The domain every table is stored under in Single mode.
ru/adminPage.json::adminPage.defaultSamp: Row ceiling applied to sampled queries, such as previews and profiling.
ru/adminPage.json::adminPage.defaultTtlH: How long a cached response is served before the query is run again.
ru/adminPage.json::adminPage.maxObjectDe: How deep introspection follows nested objects when mapping a remote GraphQL schema into tables.
ru/adminPage.json::adminPage.maxListDept: Nesting depth at which list fields stop being followed.
ru/adminPage.json::adminPage.maxListItem: The first: argument Provisa sends on a remote list field.

ru/tour.json::tour.steps.stepQualityTabl: A quality checker is just a source

🧪 A data-quality checker — Soda or Great Expectations — registers as a source. It scans back through Provisa's own postgres endpoint, so one contract dialect covers a Snowflake table, an Iceberg table and a Mongo collection alike. Its results land as an ordinary table: expand the row and open it like any other.
ru/tour.json::tour.steps.stepQualityPane: ✅ Write the contract by hand or build checks column by column — null rates, row counts, ranges, freshness — and dry-run it before saving. Every scan appends, so this table is the quality history: chart it, alert on it, join it to anything.
